Financial analytics / NLP / Model evaluation

Financial News Sentiment Analysis

Built a financial-text classification pipeline using two different targets: annotated sentiment in Financial PhraseBank and market-return-based labels in WSJ89. Compared traditional NLP features, MPNet embeddings and Llama 3.1 to evaluate accuracy, class-level errors and the limits of news sentiment as a market signal.

83.7% PhraseBank · MPNet + MLP
61.6% WSJ89 · MPNet + GaussianNB

Held-out test accuracy (80/20 split); different datasets and label definitions.

PythonpandasspaCyscikit-learnTF-IDFMPNetMLPLlama 3.1
Explore methodology & results
  • Extracted and merged WSJ89 article text with supplied labels; cleaned financial text by decoding HTML, removing URLs and numbers, and applying spaCy tokenization, stop-word removal and lemmatization.
  • Engineered normalized count-frequency features, TF-IDF n-grams and 768-dimensional MPNet sentence embeddings with attention-mask mean pooling and L2 normalization.
  • Compared Gaussian Naive Bayes and multilayer perceptron (MLP) classifiers using 80/20 train-test splits, five-fold cross-validation, per-class precision/recall and confusion matrices; also examined top features.
  • Best held-out Financial PhraseBank result: 83.71% accuracy with MPNet + MLP (three text-sentiment classes). Best WSJ89 result: 61.59% with MPNet + GaussianNB (binary return-based labels).
  • Benchmarked Llama 3.1 through an inference API: 76% accuracy on 25 PhraseBank items; on the same 25 WSJ89 articles, MPNet + GaussianNB scored 64% versus Llama's 32% under a three-label prompt.
  • Key insight: linguistic tone and market-return labels capture different targets. The work benchmarks classification methods; it does not claim to forecast returns or validate a trading strategy.

SQL / Database Analytics

Airline Operations & Customer Analytics

Developed PostgreSQL queries and Python database methods for an airline travel system, transforming relational booking and flight data into operational KPIs and customer segments.

SQLPostgreSQLPythonpsycopg2CTEsJoins
Explore SQL analysis & implementation
  • Built airline-level KPI queries covering route counts, average departure delays and booked ticket prices by cabin class using multi-table joins and aggregations.
  • Segmented frequent flyers using distinct country visits, booking activity across years and an inactivity filter.
  • Used recursive SQL to find airports unreachable through the route network, alongside Python–PostgreSQL methods for booking and aircraft reassignment.
  • Implemented conditional price updates and aircraft decommissioning queries; database prototype, not a deployed airline platform.

Power BI / DAX / Dimensional Modeling

Oura Ring — Business Intelligence & Time-Series Analytics

Adapted a wearable-data analytics pipeline into a Power BI portfolio case study. Structured sleep, activity, heart-rate and readiness observations into a dimensional model, then defined DAX KPIs, rolling-period comparisons and source-quality monitoring. The public demonstration uses synthetic data only.

Power BIPower Query MDAXDimensional ModelingPython ETLTime-Series AnalyticsData Quality
Explore BI model & methodology
  • Normalized daily and hourly observations into date, hour and metric dimensions plus sleep, activity, stress, heart-rate, signal and data-coverage fact tables.
  • Defined 8 single-direction model relationships and 29 DAX measures for time intelligence, weighted heart rate, rolling comparisons, dynamic KPIs and data completeness.
  • Designed four report pages: Executive Overview, Sleep & Recovery, Activity & Intraday, and Data Quality & Signals, with filters and trend visualizations.
  • Created a reproducible Python-to-CSV-to-Power BI workflow and a privacy-safe synthetic demo. The personal export was too small and had insufficient stress-label diversity for a valid supervised stress classifier.
  • Power BI project files were checked structurally, but the report has not yet been opened and validated in Power BI Desktop. The linked browser demo is a separate interactive preview.

Data Structures & Algorithms / MIPS Assembly

Columns — Algorithms & Memory Representation

Worked on a Columns-style puzzle game in MIPS Assembly, representing a 6 × 13 board as structured cell records. Implemented directional three-gem matching, collision detection, gem removal and gravity updates, alongside keyboard controls and difficulty-based game progression.

MIPS AssemblyGrid TraversalArrays & RecordsPattern MatchingCollision DetectionGravity Simulation
Explore algorithms & implementation
  • Represented the 6 × 13 board as an array of 78 (x, y, color) records, using fixed-width word offsets and linear searches to read and update cell states.
  • Traversed the grid vertically, horizontally and in both diagonal directions to detect runs of three matching colors, recording their coordinates for subsequent removal.
  • Implemented collision-aware left, right and downward movement, plus cyclic rotation of the three active gems, using conditional branches and bitmap-state lookups.
  • Removed matched gems and applied repeated downward-alignment passes to fill gaps; implemented an automatic gravity counter that accelerates as pieces are placed.
  • Managed game state with score updates, three selectable difficulty levels, a single-slot hold/swap feature, pause/resume and restart controls.
  • Used memory-mapped keyboard and bitmap I/O, pointer arithmetic for display addresses, and modular subroutines with register and stack management.

Algorithmic focus: multidirectional scanning, structured arrays, state transitions and grid updates.

Community data / Privacy by design / Hackathon

CommonLens — Community surveys, told safely

Thinking about community. Latino and Hispanic organizations in Canada collect surveys, but rarely have an analyst to turn the results into something members can read, and sharing raw answers can expose the people who gave them. CommonLens turns a survey file into a privacy-safe, plain-language data story in English, Spanish or French.

I built it solo for the Vibe Coding Hackathon at Building Our Future in AI: The Latin@ Summit, organized by Alianza Latina (Toronto, October 2026), and presented it to the judges.

5Smallest group ever shown
3Languages: EN · ES · FR
0Servers that see the raw data
LovableReactTailwind CSSPapaParseRechartsWilson intervalsPrivacy by design
Explore how it works
  • Privacy guard: detects and removes identifier columns (names, emails, phone numbers) and never shows a group of fewer than 5 people, so no one can be singled out.
  • Story builder: compares groups, ranks the largest differences and turns each into a card with a plain-language headline, a chart and a 95% Wilson range (“likely between X% and Y%”), so small samples are not over-read.
  • Transparency: every card shows the exact counts behind its numbers, and the story ends by stating what the data cannot tell you: who is missing, and why a difference is not a cause.
  • Privacy by architecture: runs entirely in the browser, with no backend and nothing uploaded. No AI reads the data; the text is generated from templates, so every number matches its chart.
  • Hackathon theme: Community-Owned Data & Shared Insights → Community data stories. The judges asked how it compares with SurveyMonkey, where the backend is and how to stop bad uploads; those questions shape the next version.
  • Next: import responses directly from Google Forms and Sheets, compare results with Statistics Canada data, and add AI-written summaries that are checked against the computed numbers.
